newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia economists say EU ratification vital.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia economists say EU ratification vital.

text.p: Slovenian economists on Monday warned of grave consequences for the economy if Slovenia failed to ratify an association agreement with the European Union by the middle of June.
"It would be a catastrophy if politicians obstruct our our way to joining the EU," Jozko Cuk, head of the Chamber of Economy, told investors at a conference.
"That would increase the tariffs our exporters pay, force many companies to slash their workforce and thus bring social unrest," he said.

Slovenia's parliament last week postponed a vote on whether to ratify the association accord for a week to allow more time to discuss parties' positions on joining the EU and changes to the constitution.

Under the terms of the association accord, which was signed in June last year, Slovenia agreed to change the constitution to allow foreigners to own real estate in the country within four years of the accord taking effect.
But recently opposition parties said ratification could contravene the constitution unless the real estate ownership rules are amended beforehand.
The Constitutional Court is due to rule on the matter later this week. The parliament said it would wait for the court verdict before taking the vote.

European Commission President Jacques Santer said in April that Slovenia's speedy ratification was a precondition for the country to be included in the first round of nations to start negotiation on EU membership, probably in early 1998.

"If we fail to join the EU that would harm the stability of our economy as our companies would lose the EU markets. I see no other favourable alternative for Slovenia," Minister of Economic Relations and Development Marjan Senjur said.

The EU is Slovenia's major trading partner, accounting for almost 70 percnet of its trade. From January this year trade with the EU has been facilitated by an interim agreement, which will be valid until the association accord takes effect.
Analysts said a delay in ratification would also hurt Slovenia's bid to be included in the first wave of NATO expansion, expected in 1999.
"Any delay in ratification is harmful and has a negative effect also on other integration processes of Slovenia," said Drasko Veselinovic, head of the Ljubljana bourse.
Traders say a delay could push prices down significantly.
"If the agreement is not ratified in the next three weeks the SBi index will fall at least 10 to 20 percent and possibly even up to 50 percent by September," a trader said.
"Failure to ratify the accord could scare international investors away for a year or more," he added.
Since Wednesday, when parliament postponed the ratification, the blue-chip SBI index fell 1.64 percent to 1,297.79.
